lead: On the eve of the Second Sunday after Pentecost, which our Church keeps as Vocations Day, the readings speak of those whom Christ calls. Paul tells Titus to appoint elders in every town of Crete and describes what a bishop, “God's steward”, must be. In the Gospel Jesus turns to the large crowds following him and tells them plainly what discipleship costs. The key words are steward and cross.

set: The letter to Titus belongs with 1 and 2 Timothy to the Pastoral Letters, written to Paul's co-workers about the life and leadership of the churches. They name Paul as their author. Many scholars think they were written by a disciple of Paul in his name some years after his death; others hold that Paul wrote them near the end of his life. The Church receives them as inspired Scripture whichever view is taken.

Titus was a Greek convert who worked closely with Paul (Galatians 2:1–3; 2 Corinthians 8:23). The letter says Paul left him in Crete to finish organizing the churches there. In these verses the words “elder” (v. 5) and “bishop” (v. 7) seem to describe the same office. By the time of St Ignatius of Antioch, around AD 110, the threefold ministry of one bishop with presbyters and deacons is clearly in place.
str: v. 5: Titus's task: set things in order and appoint elders in every town.
v. 6: the elder's home life: blameless, married once, believing children.
vv. 7–8: the bishop as God's steward: five faults he must not have, six virtues he must have.
v. 9: he must hold firmly to the trustworthy word, to teach and to correct.
kw: The word for a senior member of a community, taken over from the elders of Jewish synagogues. From it come “presbyter” and, in English, “priest”.
Literally one who watches over. The Lord himself is called “the shepherd and guardian (episkopos) of your souls” (1 Peter 2:25). The bishop watches over the flock in his name.
The manager of a household, who runs what belongs to his master and will give an account. The bishop is not the owner of the Church. She belongs to God.
vv: I left you behind in Crete for this reason, so that you should put in order what remained to be done, and should appoint elders in every town, as I directed you:
A young church needs shepherds. Paul does not leave their choice to chance, and he gives authority to Titus to appoint them.
For a bishop, as God’s steward, must be blameless;
Blameless does not mean sinless. It means a man whose life gives no fair ground for accusation, so that the Gospel is not discredited through him.
but he must be hospitable, a lover of goodness, prudent, upright, devout, and self-controlled.
Hospitality comes first. In the early Church travelling Christians depended on it, and the bishop's house was to be open to them.
He must have a firm grasp of the word that is trustworthy in accordance with the teaching,
The shepherd's first strength is not his personality but his fidelity to the apostolic teaching he has received.
ch: The Catechism teaches that, so that the mission entrusted to them might continue after their death, the apostles appointed collaborators and successors, and that the bishops are the successors of the apostles by divine institution (CCC 861–862). On “married only once”, it notes that in the Eastern Churches a different discipline from the Latin Church has been kept for many centuries: bishops are chosen only from among celibates, while married men may be ordained deacons and priests (CCC 1580). Paul's list is also a mirror for every Christian home, where hospitality, self-control and love of goodness are first learned, and where vocations are born.

r.h: Whoever does not carry the cross cannot be my disciple
set: Jesus is on the long journey to Jerusalem that began in 9:51. He has just told the parable of the great dinner, where the invited guests make excuses: a field, oxen, a marriage (14:15–24). Now large crowds are travelling with him, and he turns to tell them what it means to follow. The verses that come next, about building a tower and a king going to war, ask the hearer to count the cost (14:28–33).
str: v. 25: the crowds, and Jesus turning to them.
v. 26: the first condition: to put him above every family bond, and above life itself.
v. 27: the second condition: to carry the cross and follow.
kw: A Semitic way of speaking that means to love less, to put in second place. In Genesis, Jacob “loved Rachel more than Leah” (Genesis 29:30), and the next verse says in Hebrew that Leah was “hated”, which the NRSV renders “unloved” (29:31). Matthew gives the sense: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:37).

Luke's word means to carry a load. Every hearer had seen men forced to carry the crossbeam to their execution. Later Luke shows the picture made real in Simon of Cyrene, who carried the cross “behind Jesus” (23:26).
A learner who lives with his teacher. The word appears three times in 14:26–33, each time with “cannot”. Following Jesus is not a matter of being in the crowd.
vv: Now large crowds were traveling with him; and he turned and said to them,
Jesus is not seeking large numbers. He turns to the crowd and invites them to become disciples.
Whoever comes to me and does not hate father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, yes, and even life itself, cannot be my disciple.
Unlike Matthew (10:37), Luke adds “wife” to the list. The demand is not against the family, which Jesus defends elsewhere (18:20). It sets Christ first, so that even family love is lived in him.
Whoever does not carry the cross and follow me cannot be my disciple.
Not merely suffering, but suffering accepted in following him. The cross is carried on the road behind Jesus, not alone.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ is the centre of all Christian life and that the bond with him takes precedence over all other bonds, familial or social (CCC 1618). It adds that family ties are important but not absolute, and that parents should respect and encourage their children's call to follow Jesus, even in the priesthood or religious life (CCC 2232–2233). That is why Vocations Day is a feast for families: the first “yes” to a vocation is often spoken by a father and a mother.

qa: Does Jesus really want us to hate our parents?

No. The word is a Semitic way of saying “love less” or “put second”, as Matthew's parallel shows (Matthew 10:37). Jesus kept the commandment to honour father and mother and insisted on it (Mark 7:9–13). What he asks is that he be loved first. Those who love him first usually find that they love their families better, not less.
rite: The Panchangam remembers St Theodosia without saying which saint of that name is meant. Her name means “gift of God”, and it fits the eve of Vocations Day: every vocation is a gift of God to the Church, and every priest, religious and catechist was first a gift of God to a family. Tomorrow we pray for those whom the Lord is calling, and for the families and parishes that nurture them.
study: Paul's list of virtues for a bishop is also a list for every home. Which of them does my family most need to grow in?
What “cross” is the Lord asking me to carry behind him this week, and am I carrying it alone or with him?
